 LIKE 1
Lakecia Benjamin: We Dream
By Mike Jurkovic
May 28, 2026
View read count
Lakecia Benjamin is clearly pulling no punches on We Dream. Not that she ever has, given a discography that includes 2020's Pursuance: The Coltranes (Ropeadope Records); 2012's intoxicating, groove-crazy Retox (Motema) or the spellbinding sister releases Phoenix (Whirlwind, 2023) and the super stoked Phoenix ReImagined (Live) (Ropeadope Records, 2024). We Dream drops the mic and leaves the rest up to the listener: What are you going to do to make the world a better place today?

Excitable and fire-breathing, Benjamin not only lets her horn prove her propers, but she also raises her voice primally, with the power of the lioness, to slash away the armor of somnambulance we have wrapped ourselves comfortably in and kicks in to the kick-ass poem "First Light." A statement-of-purpose opening statement featuring the rakish young pioneer and her equally pioneering peers, drummer Jonathan Barber, trumpeter Sean Jones, bassist Elias Bailey, and pianists Oscar Pérez and Miki Hayama.  

It is a surely dizzying moment, succeeded wantonly by the classic quarter styled "Beyond the Dream," a very now styled throwback to John Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones getting down in Hackensack, 1964 with Rudy Van Gelder getting it all down on tape. Oh, and by the way, Terrence Blanchard goes one-on-one with the leader. Jones gets his Roy Hargrove-like chill on the R&B /jazz trailblazer, "My Only."

Still, Benjamin never lets up on the petrol, bringing in Chief Xian aTunde Adjuah for a smooth call and response breakaway car chase of a track, "Mi Gente." "Ascension," with its incessant bass throb and Benjamin's keening vocal, "trying to remember the shape of peace," leads the way into a performance so vibrant it is hard to imagine how the whole thing remains tied to terra firma. Subsequently, the saxophonist's avowed avengers—Jones, sax-master Chris Potter and drummer Jeff "Tain" Watts himself—take down whatever walls remain on the combustible, hot-house frolic "DreamBreaker."

Hiromi, as suspected and most hoped for, brings her own subversive state of frenzy to that question posed in paragraph one, teaming with Potter to light the fuse of "Flamekeeper."  a buzz-bomb roll of the dice that Hiromi blows into full blown Sonicwonder mode until Benjamin, Potter, and company bring in the trad and bring on the blues with "Himori Jam," a sweet, swaggering swing impossible not to sway to.

Even if she was not a full fledged girl from Washington Heights, NY, hip-hop naturally and most organically spills onto Benjamin's grand blueprint for the music both here and ahead, and "We Dream" (featuring Tarriona "Tank" Ball) and "Right Now" (featuring Bilal and Kassa Overall) serve as beacons.  "New World," a surprisingly quiet, resolute closer, returns us once again to the nagging question of what are we going to do today to make the world a better place after hearing the daring action, urgency, and advocacy of We Dream.

 LIKE 2
Altin Sencalar: Natural Rhythm
By Andrew Schinder
May 28, 2026
View read count
Rising trombonist Altin Sencalar has positioned himself at the top of a new generation of trombone virtuosos. The trombone may not have the widespread popularity of its brass brethren, but is nevertheless a deeply compelling and versatile instrument. Sencalar has, over the past decade, proven himself as one of the instrument's finest practitioners. Having studied with, and then worked for, trombone star Michael Dease, he combines deep respect for the instrument's legacy with a raw need to muscle it into a deserved spot in the modern jazz idiom.

Born of both Mexican and Turkish ancestry and having grown up in Texas, Sencalar has, in a fairly short time, developed a rich and diverse discography, with each new release improving on the last. Sencalar's Natural Rhythm, leans heavily into the Mexican side of his heritage (indeed, he was raised mostly by his Mexican mother and her extended family). Natural Rhythm is a blistering, fast-paced exercise in Latin Jazz deliciousness; the title is accurate, as the music is all rhythm. Sencalar successfully takes the tried-and-true Latin Jazz formula, modernizes it just enough to seem fresh while still acknowledging its history, and applies it to both original compositions and standards. The record's sound is also quite big, befitting a musician reared in Texas.

Sencalar is joined on Natural Rhythm by a robust backing band consisting of Dease (this time on baritone saxophone), Alex Norris (trumpet), Sharel Cassity (alto and soprano saxophone, flute), Art Hirahara (piano), Boris Koslov (bass), Gary Kerkezou (drums), and Alex Acuña (percussion). Sencalar takes full advantage of the formidability and explosiveness of the octet while still guiding his fellow musicians through the nuances of the material. Furthermore, while Sencalar's bandmates are not necessarily known for their forays into Latin Jazz, they are nevertheless more than up to the task and navigate the tones, moods, and rhythms of the style brilliantly.

The album begins with Sencalar's version of Wayne Shorter's "One by One," a song played frequently by Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers while Shorter was a member. Sencalar effectively transforms the song's traditional big band sound into a catchy, energetic Latin mid-tempo jaunt. Sencalar also took on the lofty task of covering John Coltrane's "Resolution" (Part II of A Love Supreme (Impulse!, 1997)), certainly not an easy lift and one that could have yielded disastrous results. Sencalar's take is, especially given the revered nature of the source material, anything but a disaster. Sencalar pulls off the frankly spectacular feat by turning the spiritual opus into a joyous salsa explosion, but without losing any of the original's profundity. Hirohara's piano, in particular, provides great texture for Sencalar's trombone virtuosity, and he has a delightful piano breakdown during the song's bridge.

Sencalar's original compositions, however, are really what distinguish Natural Rhythm. Sencalar is one of jazz's brightest young composers, and his output is even more noteworthy given that he writes for what could be seen as an overshadowed instrument. "Baila de Plena," his tribute to the beat-forward Puerto Rican sub-genre plena, is simply a blast. "Descarga de Dia" contains incredible harmonies of Acuña's timbales blending with Cassity's flute. The bolero "New Life" is a tribute to Sencalar's young daughter, and the song is appropriately tender, emotional and gorgeous.
Track Listing

One By One; Reflection; In Walked Horace; Resolution; Baila de Plena; Descarga de Dia; New Life; Lament; Run Away; Settling.

Home » Jazz Articles » Album Review » Kyle Rowland: Not Holding Back!

 LIKE 3
Kyle Rowland: Not Holding Back!
By Ron Kalb
May 28, 2026
View read count
Blues fans concerned about the next generation of harmonica virtuosos can take heart with Not Holding Back!, the 2026 release from Kyle Rowland on the The Little Village Foundation label.

At 32, Rowland suggests he may be ready to step into a lineage shaped by masters such as Charlie Musselwhite, Billy Branch and Rick Estrin.

A prodigy at age 10, Rowland took harp lessons from Estrin and counts legends James Cotton and Lazy Lester among his mentors.

He wastes no time establishing his presence. The mid-tempo opener, "Convict No. 1," highlights a tenor-leaning vocal with a warm, resonant tone, alongside a blistering guitar solo from Chicago-bred Rockin' Johnny Burgin that recalls his work alongside Paul Butterfield. A Rowland original, the track balances grit with humor, as he sings, "Your love is a prison, and I'm convict number one; / You got me locked up in your shackles, and my playboy days have come and gone." His draw-note-driven harp lines—reflecting the influence of Cotton and Estrin—leave a strong first impression.

That energy carries into "Must've Been a Dream," an up-tempo shuffle featuring a full-throated, Little Walter-influenced harp solo and sharp, economical guitar work from Kenny Marchese. Rowland pushes further on the rollicking "Complete This Order," playing with a raucous abandon that, if sustained more consistently across the album, might have elevated the set even more.

"I'll Take You Back," written by Estrin—also a co-producer and three-time Grammy nominee for blues songwriting—offers a change of pace. The mid-tempo soul-blues arrangement suits Rowland's smooth head voice, which he accesses with ease. His phrasing and understated sense of irony sharpen the song's humor, as he dismisses an ex-lover with increasingly absurd conditions, concluding he will reconcile when "James Brown ain't funky and King Kong ain't a monkey," a quintessential Estrin flourish. Bassist Ronnie James Weber anchors the track with a relaxed, rounded tone, while Rowland shifts toward a chordal, call-and-response harp attack.

A similar feel informs "We're Still Friends," where that chord-based harp phrasing continues over a Motown groove shaped by bassist Kid Andersen. Polished backing vocals from Lisa Andersen and Dennis Dove add a subtle pop inflection.

Rowland's tribute to Fillmore Slim, "You Got The Nerve Of A Brass Monkey," is a showstopper in the comic-insult tradition associated with artists such as Memphis Minnie and Bobby Rush. Here, Rowland turns to piano, delivering a buoyant, hard-driving performance complemented by renowned Anson Funderburgh's crisp Texas-style guitar solos.

"E.G.O." drives forward with economical harp, gritty Burgin guitar, sharp attitude and a pointed message about how oversized egos sabotage relationships.

He closes with the folk-blues standard, "This Train," highlighting a bright upper-register harp tone and fluid phrasing that nods to the swamp-blues style of Lester.

Indeed, there is no holding back here. Rowland demonstrates command of blues harp, guitar, piano, confident vocals as well as a developing songwriting voice across a range of blues styles. The result is a compelling statement from an artist who appears ready to stake a claim among today's blues elite.

 LIKE 3
Shunzo Ohno: Live At Joe's Pub
By Jack Bowers
May 28, 2026
View read count
A string section? In Joe's Pub? Strange as that may seem, it is clearly the case on veteran trumpeter Shunzo Ohno's latest album, recorded Live at Joe's Pub in New York City. The seven-member section, led by Ohno's daughter, cellist Sasha Ohno, is not mere window dressing, as it plays a sizable role on every one of the album's eight numbers and is, in fact, the only voice heard on Ohno's gossamer "Firefly."

What better way to get the strings in gear than with "Going Home," the largo from Antonin Dvorak's Symphony No. 9, written during his visit to America in the early 1890s and better known as "Goin' Home." Ohno wrote the other seven tunes, closing with his award-winning theme, "Musashi." Together, "Going Home" and "Musashi" consume more than twenty-two minutes of the album's 57-minute playing time.

The problem with Live at Joe's Pub lies not so much with the music as with the Pub's abominable acoustics. Whether accidentally or deliberately, Ohno and the others often seem to be performing in an airplane hangar or some other bizarre venue that engulfs their sound and shackles it in reverb and other unwelcome side effects that make one want to cry "oh, no!" The audience, too, seems distant, as if it were observing the concert from some far-flung venue that is nowhere near Joe's Pub.

As Ohno surely heard the finished product before its release, one has to assume that measure of resonance was what he had in mind, so the onus is on him. While it is hard to envision how the album may have sounded without those burdensome special effects, an uneducated guess is that it would have been appreciably enhanced. But it is what it is, and the listener must decide whether that is more agreeable than annoying.

Japanese-born Ohno, whose long and impressive resume includes two Grammy awards, time with Art Blakey's famed Jazz Messengers and a solid reputation as a composer and arranger, bears the lion's share of responsibility for the success or failure of Live at Joe's Pub. While it may indeed live long and prosper, the chances of that happening don't seem to be especially good, at least not from this vantage point.
Shunzo Ohno · 07 - Shunzo Ohno - Dreamers

 LIKE 1
How Now Brown Cow: Don't Drink The Milk - It's Spoiled
By Don Ball
May 27, 2026
View read count
Instrumental funk/soul bands are often spurned by the jazz aficionados as less serious than "real" jazz bands, but that would be a mistake with How Now Brown Cow. Despite the playfulness of the band name and song titles, in addition to having a great deal of fun playing, they are serious musicians and this is seriously good music.

How Now Brown Cow has played in the Seattle , Washington community for more than a decade, often as a trio. This live recording from the Sea Monster Lounge, where the band plays regularly, showcases the improvisatory finesse of the band members, from Dave Kurtiak's thick, complicated bass runs to Donovan Pfeifer's solid groove on drums to Kerry O'Connor's funky keyboards. They are supplemented on this recording by Brad Schrandt on sax and flute, a frequent collaborator with the band. His contributions add a forceful texture to the songs and help elevate them even more.

The opener, "No Cat Having Bag," sets the tone for the album. A stomping funky number, the tune is pushed along by Kurtiak's pulsating, busy basslines and Pfeifer's stuttering stickwork, with Schrandt and O'Connor trading solos over the tight rhythm. The members complement each other and engage in keeping the sound fresh and exciting. Even when they slow it down in songs like "Pippity Poppity" and "South of No North," Kurtiak's fingers are moving up and down the bass neck to Pfeifer's steady beat, with O'Connor throwing accents from the keyboards. This is a band on the level of like-minded but better-known bands like Lettuce and Snarky Puppy.

The musical conversations they have on every song are engrossing as well as danceable, especially between O'Connor and Schrandt, working almost as call-and-response at times. The use of flute on a couple of songs offers a different, unexpected flavor. While a more muscular instrument like the sax is expected on funk songs rather than the more delicate flute, Schrandt uses the instrument on "Hang a Louie" to drive the song, while on "That Dog Don't Hunt" he lets the flute float above the cascading keyboard groove O'Connor lays down over a bouncing rhythm from Kurtiak and Pfeifer.   

Based on this recording, the band is definitely one to see live. Although the title is a bit misleading—there is nothing spoiled about this music. Drink it up and you will feel like the psychedelic cow of the cover, well-sated and a little woozy.
Track Listing

 LIKE 5
Miles Davis: Ascenseur Pour L'Échafaud
By Jack Kenny
May 27, 2026
View read count
A legend has grown up around the music Miles Davis created for Louis Malle's debut film Lift to the Scaffold (Ascenseur pour l'échafaud). The story goes that Davis arrived at the Paris studio having never seen the film. He watched the rushes once, then improvised as the footage rolled with his European quintet—Rene Urtreger on piano, Barney Wilen on tenor saxophone, Pierre Michelot on bass, and Kenny Clarke on drums. The music was recorded on the night of December 4 and 5, 1957.

The circumstances surrounding the recording are central to its mythology, and the spontaneity was real: Davis was at the peak of his powers.

The film's plot concerns the hired murder of Jeanne Moreau's husband. The professional killer realizes, after the deed is done, that he has left crucial evidence at the scene. Returning to retrieve it, he becomes trapped in the building's lift.

1957 was a landmark year for Davis. In May he had recorded Miles Ahead (Columbia) with Gil Evans. In December came the groundbreaking Lift to the Scaffold sessions—and just four days before those recordings, Davis had played a concert at the Olympia in Paris with the same musicians.

He had come to Paris under contract to appear at the Club Saint-Germain, leaving his regular group behind in New York. By this point he was famous enough to draw crowds on his own. The ensemble he assembled was formidable. Barney Wilen was just twenty, fresh to the scene but already commanding. Pierre Michelot had played with Sidney Bechet and Clifford Brown. René Urtreger was the house pianist at the club and had accompanied Lester Young. Kenny Clarke—who had helped redefine jazz drumming in the 1940s—had made Paris his home. Beyond their residency at Saint-Germain, the group also played concerts in Brussels, Amsterdam, and Stuttgart.

Writer Boris Vian captured the atmosphere of the recording session: "This recording was made at night in the studios of the Paris broadcasting station, in a most informal atmosphere. Among those present was Jeanne Moreau, the principal star of the film. She proved a very charming hostess, serving refreshments to musicians and technicians at an improvised bar. There were those responsible for the production and the technical staff, but also Louis Mall—with his braces dangling loosely—doing his utmost to encourage Miles in his musical accompaniment of the film. The orchestra members, very much at ease in this informal atmosphere, looked at images from the principal scenes and, being thus in the right mood, improvised various musical paraphrases as the reel was projected.

"In the melody 'Dîner au motel' you will notice a curious sonority in Miles' trumpet. The explanation is a strange one: while he was playing, a tiny piece of skin from his lip came loose and stuck in the mouthpiece of his instrument. Miles gladly accepted this strange new element—in the most literal sense, an unheard-of musical effect—in quite the same way as those painters who owe the quality of a particular brushstroke to mere chance."

Little preparation had been done. Davis had sketched only a few simple harmonic sequences in his hotel room and shared them with the band shortly before recording began. With the plot explained, loops of key scenes were projected in the studio while the musicians improvised directly to the images, without any pre-composed themes. Bassist Pierre Michelot later recalled: "Miles just asked us to play two chords—D minor and C7, four bars of each, ad lib." It was typical of Davis: minimal instruction paired with an unerring sense of atmosphere.

By 1957, Davis had grown weary of the dense convolutions of bebop. This challenge gave him permission to slow down—and slow down he does, the music emphasising the film's Hitchcockian tension, its fatal romanticism and nocturnal menace.

Chronologically, the soundtrack sits only months before Kind of Blue (Columbia, 1959), and in many ways it points directly toward that masterpiece. For the first time, Davis fully committed to a modal approach—accepting harmonic limitations not as a constraint but as a means of focusing on pure line, emotion, and tone. As critic Ashley Kahn has noted, "Miles liked the results, and it forever changed how he would approach music and music-making. Eventually, it also changed the jazz world."

Davis's Harmon-muted trumpet is edgy, intimate, and almost corrosive throughout. "Générique" opens the film in an evocative, unhurried mood, giving Davis space to trace the loneliness of Moreau as she wanders the streets. "L'assassinat de Carala" is dark, menacing, and brooding, coiling the film's suspense tighter. "Sur l'autoroute" and "Dîner au motel" drive hard, showcasing Kenny Clarke's crisp brushwork, Wilen's quicksilver tenor, and Michelot's fluent bass. "Florence sur les Champs-Élysées" returns to pacing and melancholic restraint.

The current reissue presents the recordings across three formats. A 180g vinyl LP reproduces the original album in a gatefold tip-on sleeve, with an English translation of Boris Vian's original liner notes. A three-10" vinyl edition expands the release to include the full original soundtrack alongside the complete session takes from December 1957, housed in a three-panel gatefold with Franck Bergerot's essay A Present from Miles Davis to Louis Malle. A limited-edition two-CD set brings together the original album and all surviving takes from the sessions of 4 and 5 December, accompanied by a 60-page hardcover book featuring notes by Ashley Kahn and Franck Bergerot.

 LIKE 1
Alexis P. Suter Band: Just Stay Live, Featuring Garth Hudson, Recorded Live At The Falcon
By Doug Collette
May 27, 2026
View read count
With the late Garth Hudson's photo on such prominent display in Debra Clark's graphic design for Just Stay Live, featuring Garth Hudson, Recorded Live at the Falcon, the participation of the brilliant multi-instrumentalist of The Band threatens to overshadow the other attributes of Just Stay Live, most conspicuous of which is the courageous choice of material. 

Lesser artists might be daunted by the prospect of covering songs by Gregg Allman ("It's Not My Cross To Bear"), Bob Dylan ("Knockin' On Heaven's Door"), and George Harrison ("Isn't It A Pity"). But also incorporating into the 11 selections comparably challenging numbers like Blind Willie Johnson's "John The Revelator" (made famous by Son House) and "Turn On Your Lovelight," the Alexis P. Suter Band acquits equally stylishly.

In fact, the latter R&B chestnut, interpreted by artists ranging from the Grateful Dead to the aforementioned younger sibling of the Allman Brothers Band, is indicative of the the overall gusto of the performances by the quintet, which so often frequents the Woodstock environs of New York State (specifically with numerous appearances at the late Levon Helm's Midnight Ramble series of concerts).

Hudson's five minutes and two seconds of solo piano is hardly an exception. Much like his spotlights on stage with his now-deceased comrades—once known as The Hawks—he is unobtrusive as he elicits sounds from the ivories that range from the rhapsodic to the ruminative, then weaves them in and out of other arrangements. 

In that sense, that cut is a microcosm of this program. Recorded (in Dolby Atmos Surround Sound) by Alan Douches at the Falcon Arts Center in Marlboro, New York, the sound is most robust as mixed and mastered by that same engineer. In fact, the subtlety of the audio fosters the resonance of the sonorous tones Suter shares with her co-singers Vicki Bell and Linda Pino on  "Whistling in the Dark."  

And yet, on this co-write of the former with Suter Band guitarist Jimmy Bennett, Peter Bennett's bass booms as much as Ray Grappone's drums rumble. Such sonic depth matches the well of emotions this ensemble draws upon during this roughly 70-plus minutes performance. 

The uplifting likes of "Rise" may be the most exalting moments here, but not by much. The devotional overtones are unmistakable as they pervade this rendition of the aforementioned Beatle's number. Accordingly, that cut makes for a logical conclusion to this set because it simultaneously sounds like a benediction from the performers to their audience and a testimonial to the power of great soul music as on display throughout Just Stay Live.

Home » Jazz Articles » Album Review » Jim Robitaille: Sonic

 LIKE 4
Jim Robitaille: Sonic
By Jack Bowers
May 27, 2026
View read count
As guitarist in a trio setting, Jim Robitaille has to wear a number of hats: melodic, harmonic and improvisational. And on Sonic, the Massachusetts-based guitarist's ninth recording under his name, Robitaille dons one more headdress, as eight of the album's ten numbers are his original compositions.

Robitaille plays his parts well, as do his astute teammates: bassist Tom Casale and drummer Chris Poudrier. Even so, there is a persistent sameness throughout the session that seems to say, "Yes, this is good—but it's not getting any better."

That may be selling it short, as everyone is clearly giving the music his best shot, and there are decent solos along the way by Robitaille and Casale (and by Poudrier on the brisk "Room 554" and Miles Davis' "All Blues"). Robitaille's themes, on the other hand, are well-meaning but several rungs removed from impressive. The same tepidness holds true for "All Blues" and John Coltrane's gentle "Central Park West," neither of which showers sparks in the hands of a trio.

The opening number, "Stratus," moves into an affirmative gear after Robitaille's subtle guitar synth intro, and Casale takes the first solo before the leader adds a few incisive remarks. "Anthem," written for the late bassist and Robitaille colleague Bill Miele, enfolds a softer tone, as do "The Sea and the Sky," "Sonic" and "Blue Moon," which follow. "Pulse" imparts some rhythmic heat before "Central Park West" again lowers the temperature.

"Room 554" is the spiciest item on the menu, and everyone digs in hard to underline its rhythmic imprint, but placidity returns on the ethereal "Sound Origins," and "All Blues," even though hearty and well-played, seems rather out of place in a trio format.

Bottom line: a good but less than persuasive session whose appeal may be limited to those who appreciate the synergy of a trio, especially one whose focal point is a guitar.

 

 
Whaling City Sound · Jim Robitaille Trio - Sonic
